beats.care: Blanket age bans on going online now face a high bar in India. Expect child modes, private-by-default accounts and stricter limits on strangers messaging teens.
beats.what: On 15 October, Justices Pardiwala and Vinod Chandran ruled that every child has a fundamental right to access and use the internet.
beats.why: The case was about platforms failing to remove child sexual abuse material. The court said punish the abusers and platforms, not the children.

cards.body: The court said keeping children offline would be to mistake the victim for the problem. It still allows targeted limits, like blocking adult sites, parental supervision and a dedicated child mode on social media.

Flagged abuse content must be checked by at least three trained human reviewers, matches to a known database removed at once, and reporting made possible in two steps. Big repeat offenders could face heavy fines.
cards.title: what must platforms do now?

cards.body: Nobody asked the court to declare an internet right. The plea, by an NGO, was about platforms not removing child abuse material since a 2024 ruling.
The Centre must report on a national database of abuse content, school lessons on digital safety and support for victims.

cards.q: According to the Supreme Court, how should kids be protected online?
cards.why: The court said blanket bans punish the victim; the fix is going after harmful material and the people and platforms behind it.

cover.label: Right to life now covers kids going online

hook: Can anyone ban you from the internet *for your own safety*? SC says no

learn.t: The court read the right from Article 21, the right to life, together with Article 19(1)(a), the right to free speech.
